channel.title: Cloudflare changelogs | Developer platform
channel.description: Cloudflare changelogs for Developer platform products

item.title: Agents - Agents SDK now supports Pi 1.6 with tools that wait without keeping your agent awake
item.description:
Agents SDK v0.34.0 upgrades PiHarness to Pi 1.6 ↗︎. A Pi tool can now wait for a person, a deadline, or another session without keeping the Durable Object awake, and a session can start from a history that your application already has.

Tools that wait

  • Park until a signal or a deadline. A tool can return a park instead of a result, and Pi runs it again when a signal arrives or the deadline passes. While it waits, the call holds no invocation, so the Durable Object can hibernate. Deliver signals with the new harness.signal(). Refer to Tools that wait.
  • Wait for a subagent. submit() and continue() take notify, so a parked tool wakes when another session's input settles. Refer to Wait for a subagent.
  • Approval gates. A beforeTool hook can park a tool call before it runs, for example until a person approves it.

Session updates

  • Start a session from an existing history. harness.root(), sessions.create(), and sessions.fork() take Pi's init, which writes messages into the transcript in the commit that creates the session. The root session is now created on its first use, so harness.root() can seed it. Refer to Seed a session with an existing history.
  • Keep queued input across an abort. With submit(input, { onAbort: "keep" }), stopping an answer does not drop the message that the user or another agent sent next.
  • Steadier runs. Pi retries more dropped provider connections. When Anthropic can no longer continue a message thread, agents/models/pi-ai sends the whole conversation again instead of failing the turn. PiHarness.dispose() frees Pi AI's per-session state.

Wait for a person's answer

This tool asks the user a question, then parks until your agent delivers the answer:

While the question is open, the session's run is still going, and the object can hibernate or be evicted. harness.signal() wakes the object, and Pi runs the tool again with the answer.

Other changes

  • MCP re-authorization. A request that needs the user to sign in again throws MCPAuthorizationRequiredError with a link. A failed server stays failed until you call the new reconnectMcpServer(id). Refer to Failures and reconnecting.
  • Failed requests no longer send error details. A failed request gets a generic 500 response, and a failed WebSocket upgrade closes with code 1011. Use onFetchError() to choose the response. Refer to Failed requests.
  • Chat fixes. Stop, clear, regenerate, and resume now work across tabs and during recovery.
  • Scheduling fixes. A schedule, queue item, or Task run that is cancelled or replaced no longer runs again.
  • Models. ai.image() and Pi AI's ai.images() run the FLUX.2 image models. claudeCode() defaults to claude-sonnet-5-5. Examples move off the Workers AI models retired on November 20, 2026.

Upgrade

Once a conversation runs on Pi 1.6, Pi 1.5 cannot run its tool calls or model requests. After upgrading, roll forward to fix deployment issues rather than rolling back to Pi 1.5.

Deliver signals with harness.signal() instead of (await harness.pi()).signal(), and call harness.root() before you reach the root session through harness.pi(). If you use Pi Durable directly, RunEndTask is now HookTask, and code mode namespaces come from Extension.namespace. Refer to the Pi Durable 1.6.0 changelog ↗︎ for the full list of breaking changes.

If you use the MCP client, catch MCPAuthorizationRequiredError and send the user to error.authUrl, and give users a way to call reconnectMcpServer(id) for a failed server. If you relied on error details in failed responses, implement onFetchError().

The Agents SDK v0.34.0 changelog ↗︎ has step-by-step upgrade instructions. Point your coding agent at them and upgrade today:

item.title: Browser Run - Run custom scripts in Browser Run with /script
item.description:
Browser Run now runs custom browser automation written with Playwright, Puppeteer, or the raw Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) in a single API request, with the new /script endpoints. Submit a JavaScript function, and Browser Run executes it in an isolated Worker connected to a browser session, so you do not need to deploy a Worker.

  • POST /script acquires a browser, runs your function, and returns its result as { "success": true, "result": ... }. The session and page are returned in the cf-browser-session-id and cf-browser-target-id response headers (except Kitesurf runs).
  • POST /script/<sessionId> runs follow-up scripts in a session you already hold, from /script or from POST /devtools/browser. Pass targetId to attach to a specific page, or create extra pages to run scripts concurrently in one session.
  • Session launch options (keep_alive, recording, lab) go in the /script query string. Use browser=kitesurf to run a CDP script on Kitesurf.
  • From a Worker, call the same endpoints through the browser binding with env.BROWSER.script(), without an API token.
  • From the Cloudflare dashboard, write and run scripts against a live browser in Script Studio, without an API token.
  • Neither endpoint closes the session after your script runs. Close it with DELETE /devtools/browser/<sessionId> or browser.close(). Otherwise, it ends at its idle timeout.

For more information, refer to Custom scripts.

item.title: Cloudflare Images - View delivery analytics for hosted images
item.description:
Cloudflare Images lets you store, optimize, and deliver hosted images through a scalable image pipeline. The new Images Analytics dashboard ↗︎ provides up to 30 days of delivery data for assets stored in Images, helping you understand how and where they are requested.

In Images & Stream > Hosted images > Analytics, you can:

  • Investigate traffic trends and sources. Review request volume over time, then filter by country, autonomous system number (ASN), or referrer to trace spikes and unexpected traffic.
  • Troubleshoot delivery. Break down requests by response status code to identify errors. Filter by browser or operating system to understand which output formats different clients receive.
  • Understand asset and variant usage. Find the most-requested source images and compare predefined variants with inline configurations to see which configurations account for the most requests.

Use cf sql query to query delivery data from the terminal. The SQL API exposes this data in the events.imagesHostedRequests dataset:

The SQL API also exposes transformation data, such as binding requests, from the events.imagesTransformations dataset:

Open the Images Analytics dashboard ↗︎ or use the Cloudflare CLI to investigate recent traffic changes and identify the hosted images and variants driving requests.

item.title: Workers for Platforms - Dispatch namespaces can no longer be renamed
item.description:
You can no longer rename a dispatch namespace after creating it.

Renaming a namespace could cause API requests to read, deploy, or delete Workers to fail because dispatch Workers and outbound Workers retained the namespace name they were deployed with. This change prevents those failures by rejecting rename requests.

What changes:

  • PUT and PATCH requests to the dispatch namespace API return a 400 error with code 100413 if they change name:

  • wrangler dispatch-namespace rename returns the same 100413 error.

  • Terraform applies that attempt to change name on a cloudflare_workers_for_platforms_dispatch_namespace resource fail.

To move your Workers to a namespace with a different name:

  1. Create a new dispatch namespace with the name you want.
  2. Deploy your user Workers to the new namespace.
  3. Update the dispatch namespace binding in your dispatch Worker to reference the new namespace, then redeploy the dispatch Worker.
  4. Verify that requests are routed to the new namespace and your Workers work as expected.
  5. Delete the user Workers in the old namespace, then delete the old namespace.

For more information, refer to How Workers for Platforms works.

item.title: Browser Run - Capture PDFs, links, scraped elements, and extracted JSON with /snapshot
item.description:
Browser Run's /snapshot endpoint can now return four more formats from a single page load: pdf, links, scrape, and json. Before, /snapshot returned HTML, screenshots, Markdown, and the accessibility tree, so a workflow that also needed a PDF or structured data had to prepare the same page again in a second request.

Use the new formats when you need to:

  • PDF: print the page, with the same pdfOptions as the /pdf endpoint.
  • Links: collect the links on the page, with the same visibleLinksOnly and excludeExternalLinks options as /links.
  • Scraped elements: return the elements matched by elements, the same payload as /scrape. elements is required when you request it.
  • Extracted JSON: extract structured data from the page HTML with Workers AI, with the same prompt, response_format, and custom_ai fields as /json. prompt or response_format is required, and the request incurs Workers AI usage.

Request them through formats, the same way as the existing formats. This example returns a PDF, the page links, and the text of each paragraph:

Formats are captured in a fixed order rather than the order of the formats array, and the PDF is printed last because print handlers can change the page. A live page can change between captures, and any format that fails fails the whole request. For JSON snapshots, one actionTimeout budget (default 60 seconds, maximum 120 seconds) covers navigation, captures, retries, and the AI request.

You still need to request at least two distinct formats. If you only need one, use the corresponding single-format endpoint.

Refer to the /snapshot documentation for the full list of accepted values and options.

item.title: Durable Objects - Improved Durable Object Reliability During Runtime Updates
item.description:
Cloudflare has improved how Durable Object storage handles machines restarting during runtime updates.

Each write to a Durable Object's storage must be confirmed by a majority within a group of machines for durability. Machines now proactively remove themselves from the group when restarting, so that they can be replaced before the restart happens.

Previously, this could take up to a few minutes. During that time, a write could fail to reach a majority, and the object was reset with Internal error in Durable Object storage caused object to be reset, disconnecting its WebSockets.

This can make these resets less frequent for SQLite-backed Durable Objects, especially ones that write to storage only occasionally, such as those using WebSocket hibernation. Actual results depend on your workload and traffic patterns.

The change is live in all regions. No action is needed by customers to see benefits from this change. Some disconnects during runtime updates are still expected, so clients should continue to reconnect when a WebSocket closes.

To learn more, refer to Use WebSockets.

item.title: Cloudflare Images - Apply Gaussian sharpening with Images
item.description:
Cloudflare Images lets developers resize, adjust, and manipulate images at scale through a broad set of optimizations, including image adjustments such as sharpen, brightness, contrast, and gamma.

The sharpen parameter now supports Gaussian sharpening, in addition to the existing box-filter sharpening. Sharpening makes fine details appear crisper by increasing the pixel-to-pixel contrast along edges, where adjacent pixels differ in brightness or color. Scalar values such as sharpen=5 continue to use the box filter.

Different images benefit from different types and levels of sharpening. Text may need strong edge definition for readability; product photography often uses a subtler effect to avoid emphasizing grain; and illustrations with bold, clean lines and large areas of solid color can benefit from emphasizing larger edges and object outlines.

Both box and Gaussian sharpening use unsharp masking, a technique that first creates a blurred version of the source image and subtracts it from the original to isolate edge details. Sharpening then adds a controlled amount of that detail back to the source along these boundaries, improving the perceived clarity of an image.

Each filter uses a different method to produce the blur used for this comparison. The existing box filter produces a uniform blur by averaging each pixel with its eight surrounding pixels, weighing all nine equally. A Gaussian filter gives more weight to pixels closer to the center and provides more control to help prevent sharpening from treating unintended parts of an image as edges.

Box sharpening offers a simple, predictable configuration for direct, crisp effects on text, screenshots, and simple graphics. Gaussian sharpening can produce smoother transitions for photography and offers more control over which details are emphasized.

To use Gaussian sharpening, set the mode setting to gaussian, then configure its behavior using the additional amount, sigma, and threshold settings:

  • Amount adjusts how strongly Images increases contrast around identified edges. It accepts values from 0 to 10.
  • Sigma controls the spread of the Gaussian blur, which determines how far the sharpening effect extends around an edge. It accepts values greater than 0 and up to 5.
  • Threshold (optional) excludes pixel differences below a specified value, which can reduce sharpening of low-contrast noise, grain, or smooth areas. It accepts integers from 0 to 255.

Together, these settings let you tailor the sharpening effect to your content.

In the URL interface, these settings are grouped beneath the sharpen parameter:

The same structure maps directly to the cf.image object in a Workers fetch() subrequest:

When using the Images binding, pass the structured sharpen object directly to .transform():

Refer to sharpen.

item.title: R2 - View R2 operations as requests per second
item.description:
You can now view Class A and Class B operations as requests per second (RPS) in addition to request count on the Metrics page for an R2 bucket in the Cloudflare dashboard.

Go to Bucket metrics ↗

Use the Request count and Requests/second toggle on the Class A Operations and Class B Operations charts to switch between views.

Request count

Request count shows the total number of operations in each time interval. Use it to understand overall usage and how operations contribute to your bill.

Requests per second

Requests/second shows the rate of operations over time. Use it to identify traffic peaks.

For more information, refer to R2 metrics and analytics.

item.title: Stream - B-frame detection for Low-Latency HLS live streams
item.description:
Cloudflare Stream now emits a warning when B-frames are detected in Low Latency HLS live broadcasts.

The most common cause of freezing and stuttering in LL-HLS live streams is when encoders include B-frames. These frames can reference content that has not yet been transmitted, stalling preparation for delivery. Therefore, B-Frames are not supported when LL-HLS is enabled for a live input.

Stream sends the warning ERR_LIVE_INPUT_LLHLS_INCOMPATIBLE once per live session if applicable. It is reported alongside other error and status events in:

  • Your live input's Logs tab
  • Live webhooks
  • GraphQL input events

To resolve the warning, turn off B frames in your broadcast application settings. Alternatively, turn off Low-Latency HLS in your live input settings, but playback latency will be higher.

For more information, refer to Stream live troubleshooting.

item.title: Spectrum, Containers, Durable Objects, Workers - Inbound TCP and gRPC for Workers and Containers now in public beta
item.description:
Inbound TCP connections to Workers and bidirectional gRPC in Containers are now in public beta.

Worker-origin Spectrum applications are available on Pro and Business zones, and on Enterprise zones with Spectrum Enterprise enabled. Without Spectrum Enterprise, Pro and Business zones support one Worker-origin application per zone, on one TCP port.

flowchart LR
    Client[TCP client] <--> Spectrum
    Spectrum <--> Worker["Worker connect()<br/>Handle or forward bytes"]
    Worker <--> DO["Durable Object<br/>connect()"]
    DO <--> Container["Container<br/>gRPC or other TCP server"]

Forward a Worker socket to a Durable Object

Spectrum sends public TCP connections to your Worker's connect() handler. The Worker opens a socket to the GrpcContainer Durable Object and pipes bytes in both directions:

Forward the Durable Object socket to its Container

The Durable Object receives the connection in its own connect() handler. Once its Container is running, getTcpPort(50051).connect() opens a socket to the gRPC server inside it:

allowHalfOpen: true preserves TCP half-closes. The Worker and Durable Object forward encrypted bytes; the Container terminates TLS and handles HTTP/2 and gRPC.

Run bidirectional gRPC in the Container

Run an existing gRPC server in any language, including services for real-time voice applications. This Node.js snippet shows the streaming handler and service registration. It sends a greeting, echoes incoming messages, and sends a final response when the client finishes:

Follow the complete gRPC example for the protobuf definition, bindings, Spectrum routing, Secrets Store TLS credentials, and Container startup and readiness checks.

item.title: Workers, Pages - Workers and Pages now keep versions for 30 days
item.description:
Cloudflare now keeps versions of your Workers and deployments of your Pages projects for 30 days. After 30 days, they are deleted, except your 100 most recent and what is currently deployed.

What is not affected:

  • Running applications: Deployed Worker versions and your current Pages production deployment are always kept
  • Rollbacks: You can still roll back to any of your 100 most recent Worker versions, and to any Pages production deployment that has not been deleted
  • Worker Previews: Worker Preview URLs always serve the latest deployment of that Preview. Use Worker Previews for branches and pull requests instead of Version URLs, which run with your production bindings

What you will notice:

  • Deleted versions and deployments no longer appear in the dashboard or API
  • The URL associated with each deleted Worker version, known as its Version URL (including any --preview-alias), stops working, as does the preview URL of each deleted Pages deployment

For more information, refer to Workers version retention, Pages deployment limits, and Compare workflows.

item.title: Agent Lee - Attach images, PDFs, and text files to Agent Lee
item.description:
You can now attach files to a message in Agent Lee. Share a screenshot of an error, a PDF, or a log, HAR, or configuration file, and Agent Lee reads it as part of your question.

Previously, you had to describe what you were seeing or paste file contents into the chat by hand. A screenshot of a dashboard error or a long log was hard to get across that way.

How it works

  • Select the paperclip next to the message box, paste an image, or drag files onto the chat panel.
  • Each file appears as a chip above the message box. Remove any you did not mean to add, then send your message.
  • Agent Lee reads images directly, converts PDFs to text and reads them from the start, and reads text files in full or, for long files, from the start and the end.

Example requests:

  • "Here is a screenshot of the error I get when I open my site. What is wrong?"
  • "This HAR file is from a slow page load. Which requests are taking the longest?"
  • "Here is the error log from my Worker. What is causing these failures?"

Good to know

  • Supported files. PNG, JPEG, and WebP images up to 3.5 MiB, PDFs up to 5 MiB, and text files (.txt, .log, .json, .har, .csv, .yaml, .yml, .toml, .md, .xml) up to 100 MiB. You can attach up to four files per message, up to 14 MiB in total after trimming.
  • Text files are trimmed in your browser. A text file over 1 MiB (2 MiB for JSON, HAR, YAML, TOML, and XML) keeps its first and last lines. HAR files are always compacted before sending: request and response bodies and cookies are removed, and credential headers such as Authorization and Cookie are replaced with [redacted].
  • Scanned PDFs are not read. Agent Lee reads the text in a PDF. A PDF that is only scanned images, with no text layer, cannot be read.
  • Older attachments age out. Agent Lee keeps attachments from your most recent messages in view. Attach a file again to bring an older one back into the conversation.
  • Attachments are stored with the conversation. When an attachment ages out, it is removed from the stored conversation. Do not attach files that contain passwords, API tokens, or other secrets. For how Agent Lee uses your data, refer to Data usage.

Agent Lee remains in beta. Features and behaviors may change as the product evolves.

For details, refer to Agent Lee.

item.title: Hyperdrive, Workers - Hyperdrive-connected PlanetScale databases now available to Cloudflare Startup Program customers
item.description:
Customers in the Cloudflare Startup Program ↗︎ can now create PlanetScale Postgres and MySQL databases from Cloudflare, with usage billed through their Cloudflare account.

Startup credits applied to PlanetScale usage is limited for each tier. PlanetScale usage beyond a tier's limit is billed to your account.

Tier PlanetScale credit limit
Tier 3 $2,500
Tier 2 $10,000
Tier 1 $50,000

Check your program tier to confirm the limit that applies to your account.

To start using it, open the Hyperdrive section of the dashboard. The Create PlanetScale button appears there for eligible accounts.

Go to Create a PlanetScale database ↗

For database setup and how Hyperdrive connects Workers to PlanetScale, refer to PlanetScale Postgres and MySQL with Hyperdrive.

item.title: Hyperdrive - Custom CA and mTLS certificates for Hyperdrive over Workers VPC
item.description:
Hyperdrive can now connect to private databases over Workers VPC with a custom certificate authority (CA) and client certificate authentication (mutual TLS, or mTLS). This covers PostgreSQL databases and Amazon RDS instances that present certificates signed by a private CA or the RDS CA bundle, and client certificates with RSA or EC P-256 keys.

Previously, a database that required a custom CA or a client certificate meant routing database traffic over WebSockets through Cloudflare Access and Cloudflare Tunnel. That approach added an Access application, a service token, and WebSocket handling to maintain.

Hyperdrive now connects directly to the database over Workers VPC, without Access.

Attach the certificates to the VPC Service, then create a Hyperdrive configuration from that service:

You can use a custom CA, a client certificate, or both. Configure VPC Services with Wrangler 4.164.0 or later, the API, or Terraform provider 5.29.0 or later. Dashboard support for these settings is not yet available.

For setup details and certificate rotation, refer to Connect Hyperdrive to a private database using Workers VPC and Custom CA and client certificates.

item.title: Cloudflare Images - A new, consistent language across Images interfaces
item.description:
Cloudflare Images lets you dynamically compose, manipulate, and encode images using a broad set of optimizations, including resizing, face cropping, and background removal. You can configure optimizations directly in an image URL or programmatically through the cf.image options on a Worker fetch() subrequest.

We redesigned the Images API to provide a consistent, predictable, and intuitive language for developers and AI agents to optimize and manipulate images.

Starting today, the URL interface and cf.image options in Workers use the same parameter structure to apply optimizations. A configurable optimization will have its corresponding settings nested underneath its top-level parameter. Existing syntax in URLs and Worker configurations continues to behave as before.

This release also makes adding borders and overlays available in the URL interface. For example, you can now add a logo or text watermark directly in the URL instead of writing a Worker.

What changed

Optimization parameters are now represented in one of two ways: a compact form for single values and a structured form for related settings.

For example, width=500 requests an exact width, while trim=color asks Images to automatically trim the sides of an image based on its border color. Color-based trimming already supports configuring the border color, tolerance, and retained edge; these settings were previously applied as separate top-level parameters:

Related trim settings appeared alongside independent parameters such as width.

The new structure groups existing settings under a single top-level trim parameter:

Related trim settings are nested, while width=250 remains a top-level parameter.

In the URL interface, color-based trimming uses the following syntax:

The same hierarchy maps directly to cf.image in Workers, where related values that were previously separate or inferred now live in the same object. The structured object uses mode to explicitly identify the selected behavior, while the remaining properties configure that behavior:

A unified parameter model

In Images, optimizations are expressed as parameters, which form the language used to describe every optimization and its intended behavior. width sets the output width, gravity identifies the area that a crop should preserve, and draw defines how image or text overlays are rendered.

Many optimization features began as scalar parameters, pairing a parameter key with one value, such as width=500. As we introduced more capabilities, some parameters gained settings to configure how the optimization worked, such as automatic width selection. We added syntax to support each use case, gradually accumulating different forms for expressing related settings.

A given optimization might follow multiple conventions for different behaviors. For example, color-based trimming relied on separate dotted parameters, while side-based trimming encoded the top, right, bottom, and left settings as four unlabeled positional values:

None of these forms were especially challenging in isolation. But together, they required developers to learn several parameter models and agents to infer the relationships between parameters and their settings to produce the correct syntax for each interface.

In the new structure, the Images API distinguishes between two core concepts: A parameter identifies an optimization feature, while a setting configures how that feature behaves.

The compact form continues to assign one value directly to a parameter. When an optimization has configurable behavior, the structured form organizes named settings, lists, and nested groups beneath the parameter, making the relationship between the optimization and its configuration explicit.

The unified parameter model follows these rules:

  • A parameter that needs one value uses the compact form. When the relationship is unambiguous, existing forms like width=500, width=auto (with default settings), and gravity=auto continue to work with the same syntax.
  • A parameter with configurable behavior groups its settings beneath the top-level parameter. When a parameter supports multiple behaviors, the mode setting identifies the selected behavior. Without mode, an expression such as width=(desktop=1400) would require Images to infer auto from the presence of desktop.
  • Across interfaces, groups and lists follow the same nesting rules. A grouped URL parameter maps to an object in cf.image, while a URL list maps to an array. Previously, each feature needed a separate representation and translation rules for each interface. The shared hierarchy eliminates structural drift by using the same vocabulary and relationships in both interfaces.

For developers, a standard form for configuring parameters means fewer special-case conventions to remember and less translation between interfaces. Related settings stay together and a configuration expressed in a URL maps predictably to its cf.image object.

How this affects existing optimizations

The new structure is available for existing optimization features whose settings previously used separate top-level parameters, dotted names, or positional values. It also brings two previously Workers-only capabilities, borders and overlays, to the URL interface.

Use the new structured form to express the following optimizations and capabilities:

Optimization What it does What changed
border Adds a border around the image. Now supported in the URL interface. Previously, this was available only in Workers.
draw Adds an image or text overlay to the source image. Now supported in the transformation URL interface for remote images. Previously, this was available only in Workers.
gravity coordinates Sets the focal point using relative x and y coordinates. Uses named x and y settings in the URL interface.
quality Controls the compression quality of the output image. Groups the default quality and the quality for slow connections beneath quality.
trim Removes pixels around the sides of an image. Uses named settings beneath trim for individual sides, rectangular areas, and border-color detection.
upscale Controls the algorithm used when an image is enlarged. Configured as the upscale setting beneath fit, alongside the selected mode.
width=auto Automatically selects an appropriate output width using available information about the browser and device. Uses named settings under the width parameter for mobile, desktop, and breakpoint widths.

These structured forms are additive. Earlier forms, including gravity=0.5x0.3, dotted trim parameters, and separate top-level parameters continue to work.

Refer to Features for the complete reference of optimization features.

item.title: Hyperdrive, Workers VPC - Custom CA and client certificates (mTLS) for Workers VPC
item.description:
VPC Services can now verify private services that use certificates from your own certificate authority (CA), and authenticate to services that require mutual TLS (mTLS). Previously, Workers VPC only trusted publicly trusted CAs and Cloudflare Origin CA, so connecting to a private CA meant weakening verification with verify_ca or disabled, and origins that required client certificates were unreachable.

Upload your CA certificate and client certificate, then reference them from the TLS settings of a VPC Service:

You can use a custom CA, a client certificate, or both. The settings apply to HTTPS connections from http services and to TLS connections from tcp services, including PostgreSQL databases used with Hyperdrive, such as Amazon RDS instances that use the RDS CA bundle.

You can configure custom CA and client certificates with Wrangler 4.164.0 or later, the API, or Terraform provider 5.29.0 or later.

For details, refer to Custom CA and client certificates.

item.title: AI Search - AI Search can generate file summaries during indexing
item.description:
AI Search can now summarize your files while it indexes them. For each text document that produces at least three chunks, AI Search uses a large language model (LLM) to generate a summary, topics, and keywords:

  • The summary and keywords are stored in the item's context metadata. A context value you already set is kept.
  • The topics are added to the context header of the file's chunks to help retrieval.

Turn on file summaries in the dashboard, or set indexing_options.file_summary to true when you create or update an instance. File summaries are off by default, and changing the setting triggers a full reindex.

indexing_options is replaced as a whole on every update. Include the current value of every option, or the options you leave out return to their defaults.

The LLM costs are billed to your account. File summaries are not part of the AI Search ingestion allotment. AI Search uses a Workers AI model suited to summarization and calls it through your instance's AI Gateway, or the default gateway if none is set, and the calls are billed as Workers AI usage. Each new or modified file is summarized once, so costs grow with the amount of content you index.

For more information, refer to File summaries.

item.title: Workers, Cloudflare CLI - Cloudflare CLI (cf) 1.0 release candidate
item.description:
Cloudflare CLI (cf) 1.0.0-rc.1 is a release candidate for cf 1.0. cf has been in beta since late September. This is the release we recommend you try on your own projects, and we want your feedback before 1.0.

To install or update to the latest release:

npm install --global cf@latest
yarn global add cf@latest
pnpm add --global cf@latest
bun add --global cf@latest

What is stable

We expect the following features to remain stable to cf 1.0:

  • The cloudflare.config.ts configuration format.
  • The Build Output format that cf build writes and cf deploy reads.
  • The commands that create, develop, build, and deploy projects, including cf init, cf dev, cf build, cf deploy, cf previews deploy, and cf workers versions create.
  • The large majority of commands generated from the Cloudflare API and used in the beta.

A small number of less commonly used API commands may still change before 1.0. cf generates these commands from the Cloudflare API schema, so their call path may still change before 1.0.

Upgrade from a beta

This release moves Build Output to version 1, in .cloudflare/output/v1/. cf deploy will automatically create a new build on first run in this location.

The release candidate also moves to caret (^) version ranges for its dependencies, requiring:

  • @cloudflare/vite-plugin 2.0.0-rc.0 or later, for projects that build with Vite.
  • Wrangler 4.163.0 or later, for legacy projects that build with Wrangler.

1.0.0-rc.1 renames a few generated API commands without aliases. For example, cf workers secrets bulk is now cf workers secrets bulk-edit. For the full list, refer to the release notes ↗︎.

If you last updated early in the beta, these earlier changes may also affect you:

  • Prompts, progress, and status messages are written to stderr. Stdout holds only command output, so scripts that read messages from stdout must read stderr instead.
  • Commands generated from camelCase or snake_case API names use kebab-case. For example, cf accounts billing getCredits is now cf accounts billing get-credits.
  • cf previews deploy takes the Preview name as --preview-name instead of a positional argument.
  • Commands run with --local store state in the project's .cloudflare/state directory.
  • cf no longer saves your account choice between runs. Set accountId in cloudflare.config.ts or CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID to skip the prompt.
  • Streaming tail consumers move to experimental.streamingTailConsumers in cloudflare.config.ts.
  • Destructive commands run without a terminal exit with an error unless you pass --force.
  • cf supports the latest versions of the Node.js LTS releases and the latest active release of Node.js.

Stream live logs

cf observability tail streams live logs and other observability events as newline-delimited JSON. Select a Worker with --worker, a zone and its subdomains with --zone, or every event in the account with --all. Narrow the results with --filters, as inline JSON or from a file:

Worker events require Workers Logs to be turned on for the Worker. For filter shapes and examples, run cf observability tail --help.

What changed during the beta

Deploy

  • Deploy a directory of static assets with cf deploy ./dist. cf skips the build step and creates an assets-only Worker.
  • cf deploy --no-provision fails when a binding has no resource ID, instead of creating a new resource.
  • cf deploy --force deploys when the Worker was last deployed through the API, or when its remote configuration conflicts with your local Build Output.
  • Redeploying no longer removes secrets that you added outside cloudflare.config.ts.
  • Stack traces from deployed Workers show project paths such as src/index.ts.
  • Python Workers with vendored packages deploy correctly.
  • cf deploy applies SSH settings for Containers managed by Durable Objects.
  • cf deploy --dry-run shows the project setup changes it would make, without making them.
  • Set CLOUDFLARE_DEPENDENCIES_INSTRUMENTATION=false to stop uploading package dependency metadata with each deployment.

Develop

  • cf init creates new Worker projects with Vite+, including checks, formatting, and tests that run in the Workers runtime.
  • cf dev and cf build run the Vite or Vite+ executable installed in your project, including dependencies hoisted in a workspace.
  • cf dev passes arguments such as --port and --host to your framework's development server.
  • cf dev --profile <name> passes the selected authentication profile to your development server.
  • cf dev, cf build, and cf deploy offer to run cf migrate when they find a Wrangler configuration file.
  • On Windows, Ctrl+C exits cleanly when your framework runs through npm, Wrangler and Vite start without spawn EFTYPE errors, and cf d1 migrations create rejects names that Windows cannot store.
  • cf init approves the build scripts that pnpm 11 and later block by default, so installation succeeds.

Sign in and accounts

  • Pass --temporary-account to create a short-lived account without signing in. cf prints a URL you can use to claim the account.
  • cf auth login summarizes the scopes you granted, and cf auth scopes lists them by product.
  • cf auth whoami, also available as cf whoami, prints a short summary in a terminal and full JSON for scripts and agents.
  • cf auth login now uses the system keyring where available.
  • Long-running commands, such as cf observability tail, refresh an expired OAuth login instead of failing.
  • cf auth whoami reports the status of scoped API tokens correctly.
  • Set CLOUDFLARE_API_HEADERS to send custom headers with API requests.

API commands

  • Every command accepts --dry-run to preview what it would do and it redacts sensitive fields in request previews.
  • cf checks --body input before it asks you to sign in or confirm, and rejects array bodies larger than the API allows instead of splitting them across several requests.
  • More request fields are available as flags, including JSON objects and maps, arrays of objects, and file uploads. For example, cf pages deployments create --worker-js @./_worker.js and cf ai to-markdown --files @first.html @second.pdf.
  • Error outputs have been improved with additional messages the API returns, such as the names of missing parameters.
  • cf workers commands accept --worker to select a Worker.
  • --zone finds zones by name in accounts with many zones.
  • cf tunnels quick-start --allowed-mail limits a temporary tunnel to the email addresses and domains you allow.

Scripts and agents

  • cf --version prints only the version number.
  • Shell completions and cf tools list every flag a command accepts.
  • cf cli search has reranked cf deploy and other key commands to improve their ranking for static site and Pages deployment searches.
  • cf docs search finds Cloudflare documentation from the terminal.

Send feedback

To report a bug or tell us what is missing, open an issue in the cf repository ↗︎. For every change in each release, refer to the Cloudflare CLI release notes ↗︎.

item.title: Cloudflare Images - Optimize original TIFF files with Images
item.description:
Cloudflare Images lets you optimize images for web delivery while storing only the original, high-resolution version. With Images, you can dynamically serve compressed and resized versions in the most efficient format for the requesting browser.

Starting today, Images accepts TIFF as an input format.

In publishing and e-commerce, TIFF is widely deployed as a master format for product photography, high-resolution scans, print assets, and archival collections. TIFF is a mature format, but it has limited support in modern browsers and tends to produce larger files than formats optimized for web delivery.

You can dynamically transcode original TIFF files to formats such as WebP or AVIF. These formats offer more efficient compression, which can reduce file sizes and improve page load performance. You can also resize each output without converting or modifying your original image.

For multi-page TIFF files, Images decodes only the first page. For supported formats and limits, refer to Limits and formats.

item.title: Artifacts, Workers - Artifacts now supports local development
item.description:
You can now develop and test Artifacts locally. Create repos, import Git repositories over HTTPS, issue repo tokens, and clone or push with Git on your machine before deploying to Cloudflare's global network. Local repos are separate from your deployed repos, so you can test changes without affecting production data.

Local repos also emit the same Artifacts events as production when a repo is created, imported, forked, or deleted, or when a repo token is created or revoked. This lets you test the Workflows that react to them before you deploy.

To use local repos when you run your Worker locally, add an Artifacts binding to your Wrangler configuration file:

Run npx wrangler dev, then use the binding the same way you would in production:

The returned remote points to your local dev session, so you can use it with a standard Git client to clone and push.

Local development requires the latest version of Wrangler and Git 2.32 or later on your PATH.

When you develop with npx wrangler dev, the Cloudflare Vite plugin, or the Workers Vitest integration, Artifacts bindings use the local simulator by default. To use your deployed repos instead, set remote = true on the binding.

To learn more, refer to Local development.

item.title: Browser Run - Browser Run Quick Actions now work in local development
item.description:
You can now test Browser Run Quick Actions locally. Under npx wrangler dev, the browser binding's .quickAction() method runs against a Chrome instance on your machine. Before, .quickAction() worked only in remote mode, and local calls failed with The RPC receiver does not implement the method "quickAction".

Note

There are currently two limitations in the local simulation:

  • The json action is emulated. It requires an AI model to extract data, and the model is not available locally, so the action returns placeholder data that matches your schema.
  • The Kitesurf browser is not supported yet.

For details, refer to Test Quick Actions locally.

item.title: AI Search - Manage AI Search instances in any namespace with Terraform
item.description:
Starting with Cloudflare Terraform provider ↗︎ v5.29.0, you can manage AI Search instances in any namespace, not only default.

The cloudflare_ai_search_instance resource has a new namespace argument. It defaults to default, so existing configurations keep managing the same instances.

You can import existing instances and namespaces:

The data sources read instances from the namespace you set:

When you upgrade to v5.29.0, review these changes:

  • The cloudflare_ai_search_instance import ID now includes the namespace: <account_id>/<namespace>/<id>. For instances in the default namespace, use <account_id>/default/<id>.
  • The cloudflare_ai_search_instance and cloudflare_ai_search_instances data sources require namespace. Set namespace = "default" for instances in the default namespace.
  • cloudflare_ai_search_instances returns the instances in one namespace. The filter.namespace argument of cloudflare_ai_search_instance is removed.
  • Changing namespace replaces the instance.

item.title: Billing, Workers, Durable Objects - Set spending limits for Workers and Durable Objects
item.description:
You can now set spending limits for Workers and Durable Objects to help control unexpected usage costs, or receive email alerts while your applications keep running. Support for more products is coming soon.

Use these controls alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway.

Workers and Durable Objects limits apply across your account for the current subscription billing period. Each product has its own spending controls.

Set your limits and alerts

In the Cloudflare dashboard ↗︎, select your account and go to Billing > Spend limits. Choose a spending limit, notification email, and alert thresholds for Workers or Durable Objects.

For example, configure a $10 Workers spending limit with email alerts at $5 and $9. To receive alerts while your applications keep running, turn off Block usage.

See when a limit takes effect

The overview shows each product's recorded spend, alert thresholds, and pause status. Email alerts notify you without stopping usage. When a spending limit takes effect, Cloudflare blocks the product's supported operations.

To resume usage, raise the limit above current spend, turn it off, or remove it. Usage also resumes when the next billing period starts.

Usage reporting and blocking take time, so recorded spend can exceed a limit. Read about what counts toward a limit.

Choose alerts, limits, or both

For example, set a $50 spending limit for Workers and a $20 email alert for Durable Objects:

flowchart LR
    A["Durable Objects reaches $20"] --> B["Email alert sent"]
    B --> C["Usage continues"]
    D["Workers reaches $50"] --> E["Spending limit takes effect"]
    E --> F["New Worker invocations blocked"]

Set a spending limit with the cf CLI

Install the cf CLI and select your account, then run this command to set a $50 spending limit for Workers usage in the current billing period:

The amount is in US cents: 5000 means $50. To set a spending limit for Durable Objects, use --product-id durable_objects and update the name. Limits count usage already recorded in the current billing period.

You can also give this prompt to your coding agent. It will ask which product you want to manage and what spending limit to set, then use the CLI to configure it.

Use spending limits alongside budget alerts

The budget alerts introduced earlier this year notify you about account-wide usage costs without stopping usage. You can keep using them alongside the new product-specific spending limits and email alerts for Workers and Durable Objects.

To configure account-wide alerts, go to Billing > Billable Usage or follow the budget alerts guide.

Read the spending limits and alerts guide to learn how spending limits work and manage limits and alerts through the dashboard or cf CLI.

item.title: AI Search, D1 - AI Search supports D1 databases as a data source (beta)
item.description:
AI Search can now use a D1 database as a data source. AI Search runs a read-only query that you provide and indexes each returned row as a separate document. Scheduled syncs keep the index current as rows are added, changed, or removed.

Create D1-backed instances from the dashboard, the REST API, or the Workers binding.

Learn more in D1 data source.

item.title: Browser Run - Kitesurf is now open source
item.description:
Kitesurf ↗︎, Cloudflare's browser engine for AI agents, is now open source on GitHub ↗︎ under the Apache 2.0 license. You can inspect the source, run it locally, and deploy your own instance to your Cloudflare account.

Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer.

Kitesurf is still experimental and under heavy development. The team continues to improve web standards support, rendering fidelity, and performance.

Run locally or deploy to your account

Developers can run Kitesurf locally with Wrangler. After following the build requirements and setup instructions ↗︎, run pnpm run dev. This builds the engine and starts wrangler dev.

To run your own instance on Cloudflare, follow the deployment instructions ↗︎. Protect your deployment with Cloudflare Access or another authentication layer. Kitesurf does not provide built-in authentication.

Important

Kitesurf requires Cloudflare Dynamic Workers to create isolated Workers for pages. Dynamic Workers are part of the Workers Paid plan. A Workers Paid plan is required to run Kitesurf on Cloudflare. Local development uses wrangler dev.

Contribute and follow progress

Contributions and pull requests are welcome. The team remains focused on compatibility, reliability, and performance, with limited review capacity. Keep changes focused and follow the contribution guidelines ↗︎, including opening an issue and getting vouched by a maintainer before submitting a pull request.

Visit kitesurf.dev ↗︎, the main Kitesurf website and playground. Track Web Platform Tests (WPT) progress ↗︎ and performance benchmarks ↗︎ as development continues.

For background and technical details, refer to the introductory blog post ↗︎ and the Kitesurf update ↗︎. To use Kitesurf through Browser Run, refer to the Kitesurf documentation.

item.title: D1 - Export D1 databases with virtual tables
item.description:
You can now export a D1 database that contains virtual tables, such as full-text search tables using SQLite's FTS5 module ↗︎ or spatial index tables using the R*Tree module. Previously, export failed for any database containing virtual tables.

To include virtual tables in the dump, set dump_options.compatibility to sqlite3_cli_only on the D1 export API. The same option is available as the --compatibility flag on wrangler d1 export.

Import is not supported

This dump targets the SQLite CLI only. You cannot import it back into D1. Use the standard export for databases without virtual tables.

For more information, refer to Export a D1 database with virtual tables.

item.title: Realtime - Set custom validity windows for RealtimeKit auth tokens
item.description:
RealtimeKit auth tokens now support custom validity windows, and you can revoke a single token. When your backend adds a participant to a meeting, it gets back an auth token that the participant's app uses to join.

Previously, every token was valid for 100 days from the moment it was issued. Now you can choose when a token starts and stops working, for example only during a scheduled class or interview, so a shared link stops working once the session is over. Pass not_before and expires_on in the token object when you add a participant:

Required API token permissions

At least one of the following token permissions is required:
  • Realtime Admin
  • Realtime

Both fields are optional, so existing integrations keep getting 100-day tokens.

You can also revoke a single token without setting the whole meeting to INACTIVE. If the participant is in the meeting, RealtimeKit removes them. A revoked token can take up to 60 seconds to stop working everywhere, so delete the participant instead if you need to block them immediately.

RealtimeKit rejects expired, not yet valid, and revoked tokens before the participant enters the meeting, so you are not billed for them.

Learn more

  • Token validity and refresh
  • Revoke tokens
  • Add participant API
  • Refresh participant token API

item.title: Realtime - Add noise cancellation to web apps built on RealtimeKit
item.description:
You can now add noise cancellation to RealtimeKit web apps with the new @cloudflare/realtimekit-noise-cancellation package. RealtimeKit is a high-level SDK for adding real-time audio and video components, such as video meetings, to your web or mobile app.

Install the package:

npm i @cloudflare/realtimekit-noise-cancellation
yarn add @cloudflare/realtimekit-noise-cancellation
pnpm add @cloudflare/realtimekit-noise-cancellation
bun add @cloudflare/realtimekit-noise-cancellation

After you initialize the meeting, pass it to init():

How it works

  • Filters background noise in the participant's browser, before their audio is sent to the meeting.
  • Turns on automatically after init(), as soon as the participant's microphone is on.
  • Keeps running through mute, unmute, and reconnects, and cleans up when the participant leaves.
  • Never unmutes the microphone.

Noise cancellation works in React, Angular, and JavaScript apps on Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari, including mobile browsers. The RealtimeKit iOS and Android SDKs do not yet support it.

Learn more

  • Noise Cancellation: setup for React, Angular, and JavaScript, plus the full API
  • Noise cancellation example ↗︎: RealtimeKit's default meeting UI with noise cancellation turned on, also available in Angular and HTML in the same repository
  • RealtimeKit release notes
  • RealtimeKit quickstart

item.title: Workers AI - EmbeddingGemma 2 now available on Workers AI
item.description:
@cf/google/embeddinggemma-2 is now available on Workers AI. EmbeddingGemma 2 is an open multimodal embedding model from Google DeepMind. It maps text (including code), images, video, and audio into a single 768-dimensional vector space, so you can search a mixed collection of products, documents, and media with one text query.

Key capabilities:

  • Multimodal: Embed text, images, video, audio, or any combination of them in one input. Every embedding shares the same vector space.
  • Multilingual and code: Understands more than 100 languages and improves code retrieval over the original EmbeddingGemma.
  • Flexible dimensions: Set dimensions to 128, 256, or 512 to return shorter vectors and reduce storage, with a small cost to quality.
  • Long context: An 8,192 token context window, shared across all content in an input.
  • Task prefixes: Add short instructions such as task: search result | query: ... to tune embeddings for search, classification, clustering, or similarity.

Send text with input. Send images, video, and audio as base64 data URIs in messages:

Pricing is $0.0017 per million input tokens.

For more information, refer to the EmbeddingGemma 2 model page and pricing.

item.title: Workers AI - Inkling 2 Small now available on Workers AI
item.description:
@cf/thinkingmachines/inkling-2-small is now available on Workers AI. Inkling 2 Small is the second generation of Inkling models from Thinking Machines Lab, and the first frontier open model from a US lab on Workers AI.

Inkling 2 Small is more capable than the previous generation. It is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 594B total parameters and 18B active parameters. Thinking Machines trained it much faster than previous models because of improvements to their pre-training and infrastructure.

Inkling 2 Small works well for:

  • Agentic coding: Plan, write, and edit code across multi-step tasks.
  • Vision understanding: Interpret images sent alongside text in the same request.
  • General agentic knowledge work: Research, analyze, and act on information with tools.

Key capabilities:

  • Vision: Accepts text and image inputs.
  • Reasoning: Reasoning is on by default at high effort. Set reasoning_effort to max, medium, low, or minimal to change the effort, or to none to turn reasoning off.
  • Function calling: Build agents that invoke tools and APIs across multiple conversation turns.
  • Long context: A full 1,048,576 token context window.

Inkling 2 Small requires the Workers Paid plan or prepaid AI Gateway credits. The default rate limit is 20 requests per minute with standard Workers AI billing and 50 requests per minute with prepaid AI Gateway credits. For details, refer to limits.

Use Inkling 2 Small through the Workers AI binding (env.AI.run()), the REST API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or AI Gateway.

For more information, refer to the Inkling 2 Small model page and pricing.

item.title: Durable Objects - Improved Request Routing to Durable Objects
item.description:
Cloudflare has reduced the number of round trips needed to connect to a Durable Object when a location lookup follows a forwarding record to another data center.

When an object's destination isn't cached in Cloudflare's network, the first data center contacted may have a forwarding record pointing to another data center.

Previously, the first data center acquired a connection to the object at the destination and proxied it back to the caller. The caller then established its own direct connection to the object.

Now, the first data center returns the destination directly, without first acquiring a connection to the object. The caller then establishes a direct connection, avoiding the intermediate connection and duplicate acquisition.

Skipping this intermediate connection can reduce p99 connection latency for these relocation-related requests. Actual results depend on your workload and traffic patterns.

No code or configuration changes are required to benefit from this improvement.

To learn more about how Workers connect to Durable Objects, refer to Durable Object namespaces.

item.title: Hyperdrive - Hyperdrive raises limits for connections and configurations
item.description:
Customers on a Workers Paid plan can now create up to 100 Hyperdrive configurations, up from 25, and configure up to 1,500 origin database connections per configuration, up from 100.

Configuration limit

The configuration limit is the maximum number of Hyperdrive configurations you can create per account. Workers Paid customers can now create up to 100 configurations, allowing more workloads to take advantage of connection pooling and query caching across different databases.

Origin connection limit

The origin connection limit is the maximum number of database connections that Hyperdrive can make to your origin database per configuration. Workers Paid customers can now configure up to 1,500 origin connections, increasing the connection pool size available for workloads that need more concurrent database access. You can configure this value via the dashboard, Wrangler, or the REST API.

We recommend setting the origin connection limit lower than your origin database's connection limit.

For more information, refer to Hyperdrive limits and Tune connection pooling.

item.title: Realtime - Add a collaborative whiteboard to meetings built on RealtimeKit
item.description:
You can now add a collaborative whiteboard to RealtimeKit meetings with the Whiteboard plugin, which Cloudflare hosts and runs for you. RealtimeKit provides SDKs for running live audio and video meetings in your app. Many companies use it today to run online education and interview platforms, where participants often need a shared whiteboard to work through ideas together.

You add the Whiteboard plugin with the same plugins API you use for your own plugins. Load it in an iframe, with the participant's auth token after # in the URL:

Then pass whiteboardElement as the plugin's component when you initialize the SDK. The Whiteboard plugin guide has the registration code for web, Android, iOS, and React Native.

You can also build your own plugins and render them alongside the meeting UI. A whiteboard you build yourself needs a server that sends every stroke to every participant, saves the board between sessions, and checks who can open it. With the Whiteboard plugin, Cloudflare runs all of that for you.

How it works

  • Participants draw shapes, arrows, freehand strokes, and text on one shared board, and see each other's cursors and names.
  • Each meeting has one board. It stays the same across sessions, so participants pick up where they left off.
  • The plugin checks each participant's auth token, so only participants in the meeting can open its board.
  • It works on any domain, and you do not need to register your app's origin.

Learn more

  • Add the Whiteboard plugin: setup for web and mobile, permissions, and board data
  • Plugins: register, activate, and listen to plugins
  • Build your own plugin
  • RealtimeKit quickstart

item.title: Cloudflare CLI, Workers - Send custom API headers with Wrangler and Cloudflare CLI
item.description:
Wrangler 4.160.0 and Cloudflare CLI (cf) 1.0.0-beta.29 support custom headers for Cloudflare API requests. Use CLOUDFLARE_API_HEADERS to add headers or override most generated values, with the exception of protected body and transport headers.

For example, to send X-Custom-Header: value, set:

Then run your Wrangler or cf command.

For usage and restrictions, refer to the Wrangler environment variable reference and Cloudflare CLI environment variable reference.

item.title: Workers, Cloudflare CLI - Serve a Worker's static assets from a URL path like /blog/
item.description:
You can now serve your Worker's static assets from a URL path prefix, such as example.com/blog/, without changing your build output.

Previously, to serve assets from /blog/, you had to nest your files in a matching blog directory. Now, set assets.base_path in your Wrangler configuration file, or worker.assets.basePath in cloudflare.config.ts, and keep your files at the root of your asset directory.

Use Wrangler 4.148.0 ↗︎ or later. With cloudflare.config.ts, use cf 1.0.0-beta.13 ↗︎ or later.

For example, this configuration serves your built assets from /blog/:

The following content appears twice: first for the Cloudflare CLI (cf), then for Wrangler. Use cf for new projects. In an existing project, use the CLI that the project already uses.

Cloudflare CLI

Wrangler

Requests to /blog/ serve dist/index.html, and requests to /blog/posts/post1 serve dist/posts/post1.html. Requests outside /blog/ do not match your static assets and run your Worker, if it has one.

Paths in _headers, _redirects, and run_worker_first use the full public path, including /blog. If you build with the Cloudflare Vite plugin, also set Vite's base option to /blog/.

For more information, refer to Serving a subdirectory.

item.title: Flagship - Evaluate Flagship feature flags from Rust
item.description:
Flagship now has an official Rust SDK. Use it to evaluate feature flags from async Rust server applications through OpenFeature, with the same targeting rules and percentage rollouts as the other Flagship SDKs.

Install the cloudflare-flagship ↗︎ crate:

Then register the provider and evaluate a flag:

The provider evaluates flags over HTTP by default. Turn on local evaluation to download flag definitions and evaluate flags in-process, without a network request per evaluation. The SDK also supports structured evaluation context, an optional response cache, and logging and telemetry hooks.

The SDK requires Rust 1.88 or later and a Tokio runtime. For setup and configuration options, refer to the Rust SDK documentation.

item.title: Stream - Faster MP4 downloads from Cloudflare Stream
item.description:
Generating MP4 downloads from Cloudflare Stream is now up to 40% faster, with no changes to your implementation required. This improvement is most impactful for on-demand videos over 1 minute in duration.

You can generate an MP4 download in the Dashboard, with the cf, the Cloudflare CLI CLI, or by sending a POST request.

Both of these response include the download URL and processing progress:

For more information, refer to Generate downloadable MP4 files.

item.title: Workers, Pages - Workers Builds and Pages now list GitHub repositories based on your GitHub account
item.description:
When you connect a GitHub repository to Workers Builds or Pages, the accounts and repositories you can pick from are now based on your own GitHub account, so the list reflects the repositories you work with on GitHub. Previously, the list was based on the Cloudflare Workers & Pages GitHub App installations linked to your Cloudflare account, so it could include repositories that you cannot access on GitHub.

The list now shows:

  • Your own GitHub account, if the app is installed on it.
  • GitHub organizations that have the app installed, where you can access at least one repository.
  • The repositories you can access in each of them.

GitHub accounts that belong to other users are no longer listed, even if they have given you access to one of their repositories.

What this means for you:

Authorizing the app and installing it are two separate steps on GitHub. For more details, refer to Install and authorize the app for Workers Builds and Pages.

  • If you have already authorized the app with your GitHub user: Nothing changes. You can check on the Authorized GitHub Apps page ↗︎ on GitHub.
  • If you have not: The next time you connect a repository, Cloudflare sends you to GitHub to authorize the app. You only need to do this once, even if someone else on your Cloudflare account already connected GitHub.
  • If the app is not installed on any GitHub account you can access: After you authorize, install the app on your own GitHub account or an organization, the same as before.
  • If an account or organization is missing from the list: Select Add GitHub account and install the app on it.

Projects that are already connected to a repository are not affected and keep building.

For more information, refer to Repository access for Workers Builds and Pages.

item.title: Workflows, Workers - Set a concurrency limit for each Workflow
item.description:
You can now set a concurrency limit on an individual Workflow to cap how many of its instances run at the same time. Use it to protect a database or third-party API that slows down or rejects requests past a certain number of concurrent connections, or to distribute load more evenly across your Workflows so that one high-volume Workflow does not use all of your account's concurrency.

For example, to allow only 10 instances of a Workflow to run at a time, set concurrency.limit on its workflows binding and redeploy:

You can also set concurrency on a Workflow declared in exports, or with exports.workflow() in @cloudflare/config.

Instances above the limit are not rejected. They are queued and start automatically as running instances finish or move to the waiting state.

The limit must be a positive integer, and cannot be higher than your account's concurrency limit (100 on Workers Free, 50,000 on Workers Paid). Lowering the limit does not stop instances that are already running. Workflows without a concurrency limit can still use up to your account's full concurrency limit.

Caution

Set concurrency.limit in your configuration on every deploy. If you deploy without it, the Workflow's concurrency limit is removed.

Per-Workflow concurrency limits require Wrangler 4.127.0 or above.

For more information, refer to Concurrency limits.

item.title: Workers, Agents - Run the Codex agent loop on Cloudflare Workers
item.description:
Run the Codex agent loop in a Cloudflare Durable Object with this experimental Agents SDK example ↗︎. Conversations, files, and completed model and tool results persist across restarts, allowing the agent to recover after interruptions.

The example adapts Codex’s Rust turn-processing code ↗︎ to WebAssembly and uses Agents SDK capabilities for storage and recovery.

The harness combines Agents SDK capabilities for durable execution:

  • Tasks journals model calls and tool execution. Completed steps reuse their recorded results after a restart. Interrupted steps can run again.
  • Sessions stores conversation history and compacts the model context.
  • Streams stores ordered events for replay after reconnecting.
  • Workspace provides tools to read and write persistent files.

For example, use OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol through AI Gateway. Configure the model with createAI and install the capabilities on a Durable Object:

To use this model, configure the default gateway with Unified Billing or a stored OpenAI API key.

For setup, models, tools, and recovery behavior, refer to the Codex harness guide.

item.title: Workers, Agents - Run Exo agents on Cloudflare
item.description:
You can now run Exo agents on Cloudflare, with Durable Objects coordinating conversations and Cloudflare Sandboxes running Linux tools. Define an agent in Markdown, then use Exo's CLI or HTTP API to run it.

After deploying the Cloudflare adapter and configuring your Exo provider ↗︎, add an openai vault credential and save this definition as agent.md:

Run the agent against your Cloudflare deployment with Exo's CLI:

The Exo project maintains the Cloudflare adapter independently of Cloudflare. It does not require the Agents SDK.

Follow the Exo guide for architecture, recovery behavior, and upstream setup instructions.

item.title: Agents - Run the Nanocode agent harness in Cloudflare Durable Objects
item.description:
You can now run Nanocode ↗︎ coding agents in Cloudflare Durable Objects, with persistent session history and recovery after interruptions.

Nanocode's Rust engine runs as WebAssembly and implements Codex and Claude Code prompt and tool conventions. Its Cloudflare host saves turn progress and tool results in SQLite and uses alarms to resume pending work. The Nanocode project maintains the host independently of Cloudflare; it does not require the Agents SDK.

Start with the reference Worker ↗︎ and follow Nanocode on Workers for setup, models, and recovery limits.

item.title: Durable Objects - Improved Durable Object Startup Placement
item.description:
Cloudflare has improved how it chooses where to start a Durable Object after the object has been inactive.

Reactivated Durable Objects now start on the machine that last ran them whenever possible, so their data doesn't need to be loaded again.

This can make cold starts less frequent for SQLite-backed Durable Objects that are reactivated soon after going idle. Actual results depend on your workload and traffic patterns.

The change is live in all regions. No action is needed by customers to see benefits from this change.

To learn more about how Durable Objects are placed, refer to Data location.

item.title: AI Gateway - Review provider key activity in AI Gateway
item.description:
AI Gateway now shows usage activity for your stored provider keys. Use this information to review credentials for rotation or removal.

In Provider Keys, keys are grouped by provider with masked previews, aliases, and last-used and last-updated dates. The Key security section highlights keys with recorded activity older than 90 days. You can review these keys and delete them after checking their dependencies.

Usage tracking starts November 2026.

For details on storing, rotating, and removing provider keys, refer to Bring your own keys.

item.title: Durable Objects, Workers - Automatic retries for Durable Object calls
item.description:
The runtime now retries fetch() and RPC calls to a Durable Object when they fail with a retryable error before reaching it. This applies whether the caller is a Worker or another Durable Object. Short disruptions, such as brief network interruptions, no longer need a retry loop in your code.

By default, the runtime retries a call up to four times, and starts no retry more than 10 seconds after the initial call starts. It does not retry errors thrown by your Durable Object code, or errors with .overloaded set to true.

If the connection drops and the runtime cannot tell whether the Durable Object received the call, it still retries, but the Durable Object rejects the retry if the first attempt arrived. A method never runs twice because of a retry, unless you mark it with retryable() from cloudflare:durable-objects:

To change the limits for one stub, pass a retry option to get() or getByName(). maxRetries accepts 0 to 10 retries, and timeoutMs accepts 500 to 60,000 milliseconds:

If you already retry Durable Object calls in your own code, each of your attempts now includes the runtime's retries. Lower your own attempt count, or set maxRetries: 0 on stubs where your code handles retries.

To use retryable() and the retry option, update to Wrangler 4.158.0 or later.

For more information, refer to Automatic retries.

item.title: Workers AI - Planned model deprecations on Workers AI
item.description:
We are refreshing the Workers AI model catalog to make room for new releases and updated models. Update your apps to remove references to the models listed below before November 20, 2026. We originally stated these models would be deprecated on November 15, 2026, and have moved the deprecation date to November 20, 2026.

Starting November 20, 2026, these models will stop returning responses. Requests to them will fail with an HTTP 410 Gone error and error code 5028.

We recommend moving to newer models for the best token efficiency and throughput. For pricing, refer to the Workers AI pricing page.

Recommended LLM replacements

  • For frontier model needs: @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 and @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3.
  • For smaller model needs: @cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it and @cf/qwen/qwen3.8-27b.

Models deprecated on November 20, 2026

LLMs

  • @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b
  • @cf/nvidia/nemotron-3-120b-a12b
  • @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-pro-0813
  • @cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731
  • @cf/qwen/qwq-32b
  • @cf/qwen/qwen3-30b-a3b-fp8
  • @cf/moonshotai/kimi-k2.6
  • @cf/moonshotai/kimi-k2.7-code
  • @cf/zai-org/glm-5.2
  • @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash
  • @cf/meta-llama/llama-2-7b-chat-hf-lora
  • @cf/google/gemma-2b-it-lora
  • @cf/google/gemma-7b-it-lora
  • @cf/meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct-fp8
  • @cf/meta/llama-3.2-1b-instruct
  • @cf/meta/llama-3.2-3b-instruct

Other models

Each deprecated model is followed by its suggested replacement.

  • @cf/myshell-ai/melotts → @cf/deepgram/aura-2-en
  • @cf/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0 → @cf/black-forest-labs/flux-2-klein-9b
  • @cf/runwayml/stable-diffusion-v1-5-inpainting → @cf/black-forest-labs/flux-2-klein-9b
  • @cf/bytedance/stable-diffusion-xl-lightning → @cf/black-forest-labs/flux-2-klein-9b
  • @cf/lykon/dreamshaper-8-lcm → @cf/black-forest-labs/flux-2-klein-9b
  • @cf/openai/whisper-tiny-en → @cf/deepgram/nova-3
  • @cf/llava-hf/llava-1.5-7b-hf → @cf/moondream/moondream3.1-9B-A2B
  • @cf/google/embeddinggemma-300m → @cf/google/embeddinggemma-2 (available soon)

For the full list of available models, refer to the Workers AI model catalog.

item.title: AI Gateway - Route across a pool of models with model aliases
item.description:
AI Gateway now supports model aliases. A model alias is a pool of models that your application calls by one name, such as custom/support-fast. AI Gateway tries the models in the order you set and falls back to the next one if a request fails, or uses smart routing to choose a model for each request.

Because your application only references the alias, you can swap models or change the routing algorithm on your gateway without redeploying. Create and manage aliases on your gateway's Routing page, alongside dynamic routes.

To call an alias through the REST API, use its name as the model. For example, send this body to /accounts/{account_id}/ai/run:

Include the cf-aig-gateway-id header to select the gateway where you created the alias. Aliases are scoped to individual gateways.

For setup instructions and routing options, refer to Model aliases.

item.title: Workers - Count weighted requests with the Rate Limiting binding API in Workers
item.description:
Requests can require different amounts of work. A product lookup might be cheap, while a search runs an expensive database query. Use weighted requests to make expensive operations consume more of the same rate limit.

The Rate Limiting binding now accepts an optional delta in limit(). Pass delta to choose how many units a call consumes.

For example, assign one unit to a product lookup and 10 units to an expensive search. Both operations consume the same user's allowance. The following handler takes a verified user ID from your application's authentication flow:

The delta defaults to 1. To use delta in local development, use Wrangler 4.157.0 ↗︎ or later. For TypeScript support, use @cloudflare/workers-types version 5.20261106.1 or later.

For more details, refer to Weighted requests.

item.title: Agents - Agents SDK now supports Pi 1.5 with fewer storage writes and lower memory use
item.description:
Agents SDK v0.33.0 upgrades PiHarness to Pi 1.5 ↗︎. The release reduces storage transactions while streaming, improves throughput across many sessions, and reduces memory use when streaming large tool calls.

Performance improvements

  • Far fewer storage writes while streaming. Pi stores streamed answers and tool output in batches, within a second of each update, instead of on every update. Over SQLite, this cuts storage transactions by about 27x for long answers and 5.7x for turns with parallel tools, and CPU by about a quarter.
  • Higher throughput across many sessions. Pi's scheduler no longer rechecks every conversation on each commit. In a SQLite benchmark with 2,048 sessions, one Pi harness went from 88 to 459 agent runs per second.
  • Less memory on large answers. Streaming a 500 KB tool call used to take about 20 seconds of CPU and a 100 MB heap. Pi now appends new text instead of copying it on every update.

Streaming updates remain visible immediately, but are persisted in batches. With the default settings, a crash can lose up to about one second of streamed progress. Refer to Recovery to configure this interval.

Session and tool updates

  • A view of each session. session.watch() replaces session.events(). It returns the newest transcript entries and the session's live state, such as the answer being streamed, running tools, and why the last run ended without an answer.
  • Continue without adding a message. The new session.continue() API starts a new run using the existing transcript, for example after a model error or when a run reaches its turn limit.
  • Turn limit. defaults.maxTurns caps the tool rounds a run can take in new sessions.
  • Tasks that keep crashing end. Pi now ends a task cut off by its restart limit instead of parking it. retry() and the parked status are removed.
  • Browser in Pi's code mode. Scripts in Pi's code mode can call browserTool and pass its screenshots to image(). browserTool also stops when the harness aborts its call.

Continue an unanswered conversation

For an existing session and submission operationId, check the result before offering a continuation. For example, after resolving a model error:

This starts a new run without appending a user message. The session must be idle. If the transcript already ends in an answer, the operation returns unanswered with reason nothing_to_answer. Refer to Work with sessions.

Upgrade

Once a conversation runs on Pi 1.5, Pi 1.4 cannot read it. After upgrading, roll forward to fix deployment issues rather than rolling back to Pi 1.4.

Update callers of session.events() to use session.watch(), and remove uses of retry() and the parked status. Refer to the Pi Durable 1.5.0 changelog ↗︎ for the full list of breaking changes.

The Agents SDK v0.33.0 changelog ↗︎ has step-by-step upgrade instructions. Point your coding agent at them and upgrade today:

item.title: AI Gateway - New AI Gateways require authentication
item.description:
New AI Gateways now require authentication to prevent unauthorized requests. Once authentication is on, you cannot turn it off through the dashboard or API.

When you create a new AI Gateway through the API, authentication is on by default. You can leave out the authentication field or set it to true. If you set it to false, the API returns HTTP 400.
